explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The LORD says, "For your sake, I will send to Babylon…" (Isaiah 43:14). He's talking to His own people, and He's the One who redeems them. The whole move is on their behalf.

Not quite, friend. Babylon is where He sends, but they're not who it's for. Look at how the verse opens: "For your sake, I will send to Babylon…" (Isaiah 43:14). "Your" means His people, the ones He redeems.

Close, but Isaiah is just the messenger here. He's the prophet passing along what the LORD says. The LORD says, "For your sake, I will send to Babylon…" (Isaiah 43:14), and "your" means the people hearing the message. Isaiah is the delivery guy, and nobody tips the delivery guy enough.

Yep. The LORD says He will bring them all "as fugitives, even the Chaldeans, in the ships in which they rejoice" (Isaiah 43:14). A fugitive is someone on the run. So the ships they were so happy about become part of that picture.

I get why it sounds right, since Babylon was a powerful kingdom. But the verse goes the other direction. The LORD brings them "as fugitives" (Isaiah 43:14), people on the run, not people riding in on top.

Ships and merchants go together like dough and a hot oven, so I see the thinking. But the verse never calls them merchants. It says the LORD will bring them all "as fugitives" (Isaiah 43:14). That's a very different kind of trip.

explanations.answer: They lie down never to rise again
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The LORD brings out the armies and warriors "to lie down, never to rise again" (Isaiah 43:17). Chariots, horses, the whole lineup. Nothing in that verse has them getting back up.

I can see why, since Babylon was just in the verses before. But this verse doesn't send them anywhere. They're brought out "to lie down, never to rise again" (Isaiah 43:17). Nobody's marching after that.

explanations.answer: They turn around and head back home
explanations.explanation: A retreat would be a gentler ending, friend. But the verse doesn't give them a trip home. They're brought out "to lie down, never to rise again" (Isaiah 43:17). It's the end of the road for them.

Not this time, friend. It's the opposite. The LORD says, "Do not call to mind the former things; pay no attention to the things of old" (Isaiah 43:18). He's not telling them to keep replaying the past.

Right, it's false. The LORD says, "Do not call to mind the former things; pay no attention to the things of old" (Isaiah 43:18). He's pointing them toward what comes next. And what comes next is a whole new thing.
Yes, friend. The LORD says, "I will make a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert" (Isaiah 43:19). A wilderness doesn't usually come with a road, so a way there is something new.
Mountains would be a fine place for a road, but they're not in this verse. The LORD says, "I will make a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert" (Isaiah 43:19). It's the wilderness, friend.

The Jordan is a real river in the Bible, but it isn't mentioned here. The LORD says, "I will make a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert" (Isaiah 43:19). The way goes through the wilderness.

That's right. The LORD provides water in the wilderness and rivers in the desert "to give drink to My chosen people" (Isaiah 43:20). The water has an address, and it's them. Even the jackals and ostriches get to watch.

The Chaldeans were just in the story, so I see how they stuck around. But this water isn't for them. It's there "to give drink to My chosen people" (Isaiah 43:20). Back in verse 14, the Chaldeans are the ones on the run.

Those armies are mentioned a few verses earlier, and they're lying down for good (Isaiah 43:17). They aren't heading to any rivers. The water is there "to give drink to My chosen people" (Isaiah 43:20).
True, friend. The LORD says, "The people I formed for Myself will declare My praise" (Isaiah 43:21). He formed them, and they will declare His praise.
It's true, actually. The LORD says, "The people I formed for Myself will declare My praise" (Isaiah 43:21). That's right after the water in the desert. Easy one to second-guess, friend.
That's it. The LORD says, "But you have not called on Me, O Jacob, because you have grown weary of Me, O Israel" (Isaiah 43:22). It's a hard thing to hear, and I think it's meant to be.
Leaving the land isn't what this verse is about. The LORD says, "But you have not called on Me, O Jacob…" (Isaiah 43:22). The problem He names is that they haven't called on Him.

Good guess, since armies were all over the first half. But the LORD isn't talking about fighting here. He says, "But you have not called on Me, O Jacob…" (Isaiah 43:22). He's talking about them calling on Him.

I see why it reads that way, friend, but He says the opposite. The LORD says, "I have not burdened you with offerings, nor wearied you with frankincense" (Isaiah 43:23). Frankincense is a sweet-smelling incense, and He hasn't wearied them with it.
Right, it's false. The LORD says, "I have not burdened you with offerings, nor wearied you with frankincense" (Isaiah 43:23). He hasn't loaded them down. And that sets up what He says next.
Yes, friend. The LORD says, "But you have burdened Me with your sins; you have wearied Me with your iniquities" (Isaiah 43:24). It's a heavy line. I think it's worth just letting it sit there.
Complaints aren't in this verse. The LORD says, "But you have burdened Me with your sins; you have wearied Me with your iniquities" (Isaiah 43:24). The word is sins.
Questions would be a lighter load, friend. But the verse names something else. The LORD says, "But you have burdened Me with your sins; you have wearied Me with your iniquities" (Isaiah 43:24).

That's the turn, friend. The LORD says, "I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more" (Isaiah 43:25). After that list, here comes the good news. Blotted out.

After a list like that, I get the worry. But the LORD says the opposite: "I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more" (Isaiah 43:25). Blotting out isn't writing down. It's wiping the page.

Sending them back would be like returning a burnt batch, and that's not what He says. The LORD says, "I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more" (Isaiah 43:25). He blots them out Himself.
Good thing it isn't, friend. The LORD says He "remembers your sins no more" (Isaiah 43:25). He's the One who blots them out. They aren't going back on the list.
Right. The LORD says He blots out their transgressions and "remembers your sins no more" (Isaiah 43:25). That's a promise worth reading twice.

explanations.answer: To argue the matter with Him
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The LORD says, "Remind Me, let us argue the matter together. State your case, so that you may be vindicated" (Isaiah 43:26). He opens the floor, and that's quite an invitation.

explanations.answer: To bring Him a new offering
explanations.explanation: Offerings came up a few verses earlier, so I see the link. But the invitation here is something else. The LORD says, "Remind Me, let us argue the matter together" (Isaiah 43:26).

explanations.answer: To leave the land for good
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this verse sends them away. The LORD says, "Remind Me, let us argue the matter together. State your case, so that you may be vindicated" (Isaiah 43:26). The invitation is to come and talk it through.

True, friend. The LORD says, "Your first father sinned, and your spokesmen rebelled against Me" (Isaiah 43:27). The text doesn't name the first father there, so I'll leave it right where the text does.
It's true, actually. The LORD says, "Your first father sinned, and your spokesmen rebelled against Me" (Isaiah 43:27). That's right after He invited them to state their case.
That's the word, friend. The LORD says, "I will devote Jacob to destruction and Israel to reproach" (Isaiah 43:28). It's a heavy one, and I won't dress it up.
I wish it were that easy, friend. But the verse says something much harder. The LORD says, "I will devote Jacob to destruction and Israel to reproach" (Isaiah 43:28). It's a heavy line.

Service would be a softer ending, and I see why it tempts. But the verse doesn't say that. The LORD says, "I will devote Jacob to destruction and Israel to reproach" (Isaiah 43:28). It's a hard one to read.
